title: Obturator nerve compression: impaired hip adduction
vignette: A 56-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic due to worsening lower extremity pain and weakness. The patient has had hematuria and intermittent burning on urination for the past year. He has no history of pelvic trauma or surgeries. The patient has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 35 years. His urine culture is negative for bacterial growth. Urine cytology and cystoscopy confirm a diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma. CT scan of the abdomen shows an advanced bladder tumor compressing a nerve that passes through the obturator canal. Which of the following actions would most likely be impaired in this patient?

clues.note: A locally advanced bladder cancer (smoking-related transitional cell carcinoma) can invade the pelvic sidewall and compress adjacent nerves.

clues.text: compressing a nerve that passes through the obturator canal
clues.note: The obturator canal transmits the OBTURATOR nerve - the only major nerve to exit the pelvis this way - which supplies the hip ADDUCTORS.

whatMatters: The nerve passing through the obturator canal is the OBTURATOR NERVE (L2-L4). It innervates the thigh ADDUCTOR muscles (adductor longus/brevis/magnus, gracilis) and gives sensation to the medial thigh. Compression -> impaired HIP ADDUCTION. Answer B.
strategy: Identify the obturator nerve by its landmark (obturator canal), then recall its MOTOR function: hip adduction (and medial-thigh sensation). Reject actions performed by other nerves: hip abduction (superior gluteal nerve), hip extension (inferior gluteal nerve - gluteus maximus), knee extension (femoral nerve - quadriceps), and hip flexion (femoral/lumbar plexus - iliopsoas).

eliminations.label: Hip abduction - superior gluteal nerve
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hip abduction is performed by the gluteus medius/minimus and tensor fasciae latae, innervated by the SUPERIOR GLUTEAL nerve. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that nerve exits via the greater sciatic foramen, not the obturator canal. ✅ Correct if: superior gluteal nerve injury (Trendelenburg gait).

eliminations.label: Hip extension - inferior gluteal nerve
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hip extension is mainly by the gluteus maximus, innervated by the INFERIOR GLUTEAL nerve. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it does not travel through the obturator canal. ✅ Correct if: inferior gluteal nerve injury (difficulty rising/climbing stairs).

eliminations.label: Knee extension - femoral nerve
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: knee extension is by the quadriceps, innervated by the FEMORAL nerve. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the femoral nerve enters the thigh deep to the inguinal ligament, not through the obturator canal. ✅ Correct if: femoral nerve injury (weak knee extension, absent patellar reflex).

eliminations.label: Hip flexion - iliopsoas (femoral/lumbar plexus)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hip flexion is primarily by the iliopsoas (psoas via lumbar plexus, iliacus via femoral nerve). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not an obturator-nerve action. ✅ Correct if: lumbar plexus/femoral involvement affecting hip flexion.

reasoning: The obturator canal transmits the obturator nerve (the only major nerve exiting the pelvis this way)
The obturator nerve supplies the thigh ADDUCTOR muscles
Compression by the bladder tumor impairs hip adduction (and medial-thigh sensation)
-> adduction of the hip; answer B
mechanism: The OBTURATOR NERVE arises from the lumbar plexus (L2-L4), descends along the pelvic sidewall, and is the only major nerve that exits the pelvis through the OBTURATOR CANAL to enter the medial thigh. There it innervates the hip ADDUCTOR compartment - adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus (adductor portion), and gracilis - and, via a terminal cutaneous branch, provides SENSATION to the medial thigh. Because of its course along the pelvic sidewall, the obturator nerve is vulnerable to compression by pelvic pathology (locally advanced bladder or cervical cancer, or during pelvic surgery); injury produces weakness of HIP ADDUCTION and medial-thigh sensory loss. The distractor actions are supplied by different nerves that do NOT pass through the obturator canal: hip abduction (superior gluteal nerve), hip extension (inferior gluteal nerve), knee extension (femoral nerve), and hip flexion (iliopsoas via lumbar plexus/femoral nerve).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > obturator nerve (L2-L4): exits pelvis through obturator canal; motor to hip adductors (adductor longus/brevis/magnus, gracilis); sensory to medial thigh.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Obturator canal -> obturator nerve -> hip adduction (and medial-thigh sensation).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on obturator nerve/canal, hip adductors, superior/inferior gluteal nerves, or lumbar plexus? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Abduction = superior gluteal; hip extension = inferior gluteal; knee extension = femoral; hip flexion = iliopsoas - none via the obturator canal.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: obturator nerve = hip adduction + medial-thigh sensation; only major nerve through the obturator canal.

firstAid.detail: Anatomy: obturator canal; hip adduction + medial-thigh sensation.
Anatomy > superior gluteal (abduction), inferior gluteal (extension), femoral (knee extension).
Anatomy > bladder/cervical cancer can compress the obturator nerve.

memoryHook: Obturator = adductor: the one nerve slipping through the obturator canal squeezes the thighs together (adduction) - a pelvic tumor pinches it and the legs won't clamp.
